articles.title: Diesel Availability a Boost for Product Tankers
articles.summary: According to Head of Research Department, Mr. Nikos Tagoulis, “supply uncertainty is also mounting elsewhere. China suspended refined-product exports around the Golden Week holiday, following a sharp increase in diesel...
articles.body:
According to Head of Research Department, Mr. Nikos Tagoulis, “supply uncertainty is also mounting elsewhere. China suspended refined-product exports around the Golden Week holiday, following a sharp increase in diesel exports during September, leaving uncertainty over policy thereafter. Russia, meanwhile, remains largely sidelined from the export market following the extension of its diesel restrictions through October and continued disruption to refining infrastructure from Ukrainian attacks. In the Middle East, the recovery in crude exports observed has not been matched by refined products. Vortexa data indicate regional diesel/gasoil exports reached 1.12 mbpd in September, down 36% y-o-y, while flows to Europe were roughly 50% lower. Lower Middle Eastern product exports are particularly relevant for Europe, given its dependence on the region for diesel imports”.

“Across the Atlantic, the US remains a critical diesel supplier. US diesel/gasoil exports reached around 1.57 mbpd in Q3 2026, up 28% y-o-y, supported by strong flows into Central and South America alongside increasing long-haul shipments to Europe by approx. 35% y-o-y. While intra-American trades are relatively short-haul, stronger US Gulf-Europe shipments add ton miles and provide meaningful support for MR employment. Keeping US exports unrestricted also preserves a crucial source of incremental Atlantic Basin diesel supply”, Mr. Tagoulis said.

He added that “within this constrained supply environment, Europe is increasingly turning to alternative suppliers beyond the US, with India emerging as a more prominent source. October arrivals of diesel/gasoil from India are currently expected at around 228k bpd, up approximately 65% m-o-m. India is well placed to respond to the global supply deficit, supported by a large refining base fed by crude mainly from Russia and the Middle East, while New Delhi’s recent reduction in the diesel export levy provides further support for increased export flows. Strong European margins could attract more Indian barrels westward, providing further support to LR1/LR2 employment and ton-mile demand”.

Meanwhile, “longer-haul arbitrage opportunities may also emerge from Northeast Asia, with a 90,000-ton South Korean diesel cargo reportedly fixed for Northwest Europe. This trade stands out, given Korea’s traditional focus on more proximate markets such as Australia and East Asia. However, Korea’s ability to respond more broadly to stronger global diesel demand remains constrained by government energy-security measures, which cap monthly exports of regular gasoline, automotive diesel and heating kerosene at the volumes shipped in the corresponding month of 2025”, Mr. Tagoulis said.

“For product tanker demand, these developments are broadly supportive. Europe’s need to source barrels from the US Gulf, India and potentially South Korea, supports ton-mile demand across both the MR and LR segments. European strategic-stock releases could temporarily reduce prompt import requirements, but unless underlying supply constraints ease materially, the redirection of diesel trade flows towards more distant suppliers should remain supportive of tanker utilisation. More broadly, should elevated diesel prices and constrained market conditions persist, the impact could extend beyond the product-tanker market. Heavy industry, road transportation and agriculture remain highly reliant on diesel, while short-term demand is relatively inelastic . Persistently high costs could intensify inflationary pressures and weigh on agricultural economics, affecting production and exports and create a secondary spillover beyond product tankers into dry bulk, impacting seaborne grain volumes”, Intermodal’s analyst said.

He concluded that “overall, the current diesel imbalance is increasingly reshaping trade routes, as Europe’s search for replacement barrels supports longer-haul product flows. However, given diesel’s critical role in the global economy, persistently elevated prices or prolonged supply shortages could have consequences extending well beyond shipping, with broader implications for global economic activity”. Nikos Roussanoglou, Hellenic Shipping News Worldwide

China suspended refined-product exports around the Golden Week holiday, following a sharp increase in diesel exports during September, leaving uncertainty over policy thereafter.

articles.title: Russia’s shadow fleet freight rates fracture on Black Sea premiums
articles.summary: Black Sea tanker economics strengthened sharply in late September and early October as attacks on commercial shipping, disruption to Russian energy flows and tighter scrutiny of Russia-linked tonnage increased the cost...
articles.body:
Black Sea tanker economics strengthened sharply in late September and early October as attacks on commercial shipping, disruption to Russian energy flows and tighter scrutiny of Russia-linked tonnage increased the cost and complexity of moving cargoes. Baltic routes moved in the opposite direction: Aframax spreads fell further into discount territory against global benchmarks even as outright earnings rose.

The divergence reflects a growing segmentation in Russian seaborne trade. Vessels operating from the Black Sea are attracting higher compensation for security, insurance and voyage-execution risks, while Baltic routes continue to trade below their relevant benchmarks amid the operational and commercial constraints associated with Russia-linked tonnage.

The UK added 12 tankers to its sanctions list on Oct. 8, alongside measures against Russian oil companies Zarubezhneft and INK Capital.

The move followed the Joint War Committee’s decision on Sept. 16 to add the Black Sea to its Listed Areas, increasing war-risk insurance considerations for vessels operating in the region. Sanctions and attacks have not removed Russian oil from global trade, but they have changed the vessels, routes, counterparties and risk premiums required to move it.

More than 1,600 vessels linked to Russian trade over the past two years accounted for 73% of the total shadow fleet at the end of August, according to S&P Global Commodities at Sea(opens in a new tab) data. The size of the Russia-linked fleet, combined with the latest designations, highlights the widening separation between tonnage active in Russian trade and vessels readily accepted by mainstream charterers, insurers, banks and terminals.

The latest pricing reflects that shift. Black Sea Suezmaxes command the strongest relative returns as owners seek compensation for elevated security and execution risks. Baltic Aframaxes remain at the deepest discount to their relevant benchmark, while clean MR economics continue to vary sharply by loading region and destination.

Black Sea dirty tanker shadow fleet The Black Sea-West Coast India Suezmax spread for Russia’s shadow fleet against the Global Suezmax Index for non-scrubber-fitted, non-eco vessels widened to $83.36/mt on Oct. 8, from $47.22/mt on Sept. 29, according to Platts data. Platts is part of S&P Global Energy.

Novorossiysk-Vadinar TCE earnings rose to $879,766/day on Oct. 8, from $517,674/day on Sept. 29 and $493,692/day on Sept. 16. The route had been assessed at $288,088/day on Sept. 8.

Market participants said the deteriorating security environment had made Black Sea fixtures more difficult to execute. Uncertainty around vessel acceptance, insurance coverage and voyage execution has supported higher returns on trades where owners require greater compensation.

The widening Suezmax premium also came against a broader rise in dirty tanker earnings. The implied spread depends on how each Russian-linked route performs against its relevant Platts index. Black Sea Suezmax earnings strengthened relative to the benchmark, while the Baltic Aframax route lagged behind its benchmark.

Baltic dirty tanker shadow fleet The Baltic-West Coast India Aframax spread for Russia’s shadow fleet against the Global Aframax Index widened to minus $44.71/mt on Oct. 8, from minus $19.93/mt on Sept. 29, according to Platts data.

Ust Luga-Sikka TCE earnings nevertheless rose to $227,957/day on Oct. 8, from $178,125/day on Sept. 29 and $116,671/day on Sept. 16.

The deeper discount does not indicate a fall in Baltic earnings. It shows that the relevant Aframax benchmark strengthened faster than the Russian-linked route. Baltic Aframax TCE earnings have remained below the Global Aframax Index since Sept. 9.

Russian seaborne crude exports increased to 4.09 million b/d in September, from 3.82 million b/d in August, while non-G7 tankers carried 2.89 million b/d, according to S&P Global Platts.

MR clean tankers shadow fleet Russian product flows provided an important backdrop to the clean tanker market. Black Sea diesel exports fell to zero in the week to Sept. 24. Across all Russian ports, diesel and gasoil exports totaled 479,000 mt in September, the lowest monthly level recorded by CAS, according toPlatts data. The Black Sea-Mediterranean MR spread against the Global Medium Range Index for non-scrubber-fitted, non-eco vessels widened to $24.56/mt on Oct. 8, from $4.78/mt on Sept. 29.

Novorossiysk-Port Said TCE earnings rose to $108,940/day on Oct. 8, from $67,042/day on Sept. 29 and $56,458/day on Sept. 16.

Baltic clean MR discounts narrowed but remained negative. The Baltic-Mediterranean MR spread against the Global Medium Range Index narrowed to minus $4.82/mt on Oct. 8, from minus $29.56/mt on Sept. 29. Primorsk-Mersin TCE earnings rose to $42,267/day, from $26,817/day over the same period and $15,512/day on Sept. 16.

The longer-haul Baltic-East Coast South America MR discount narrowed to minus $16.88/mt on Oct. 8, from minus $41.11/mt on Sept. 29. Ust Luga-Santos TCE earnings rose to $35,041/day on Oct. 8, from $26,186/day on Sept. 29.

The divergence reflects a growing segmentation in Russian seaborne trade.

articles.title: Lower container rates are not a return to predictable service, Sogese says
articles.summary: “Europe is entering the final quarter with two forces moving in opposite directions. Capacity is becoming more available as Suez routings return, while carriers are simultaneously trying to protect utilisation through...
articles.body:
“Europe is entering the final quarter with two forces moving in opposite directions. Capacity is becoming more available as Suez routings return, while carriers are simultaneously trying to protect utilisation through blank sailings. For shippers, this means lower rates may offer an opportunity, but they should not be mistaken for a return to predictable service. The next few weeks will be defined by how quickly carriers can bring capacity back into balance with demand.” said Andrea Monti, CEO & MD, Sogese.

For a shipper, Sogese says, the working number is the delay. The report advises adding at least eight days to Far East to Italy arrival dates until Xeneta’s September scorecard, due this month, shows Far East to Europe arrivals above 20% on time. Xeneta’s August figure was 6%, a level last seen in late 2021, according to the report, and Xeneta counted 1.1m TEU held at anchor off Ningbo, Shanghai and Yantian after the typhoons. Monti’s advice to importers: “Book on the rate and date your stock on the delay.”

The rate fall is real. On Drewry’s World Container Index, Shanghai to Genoa is 43% below 9 July ($6,463 to $3,696 per 40ft on 8 October) and Shanghai to Rotterdam is 32% below ($4,933 to $3,337). Sogese calculates that a shipper moving 100 FEU a month from Shanghai to Genoa pays about $277,000 less per month than at the 9 July rate. The WCI excludes destination terminal handling, so demurrage, detention, terminal charges and inland haulage can keep landed costs from falling with the index.

A BOOKING THAT LOOKS SECURE CAN STILL ARRIVE LATE

Published schedules show more capacity than the network can deliver, the report says. A booking can look secure on the schedule and still arrive late, be rolled to a later sailing, or land together with the vessel behind it. Sea-Intelligence’s 24 September analysis supports the point: scheduled Asia-North Europe capacity across Golden Week is 27% above last year, with 12 double sailings and no blank sailings planned for the two peak weeks. TrasportoEuropa, citing Sea-Intelligence, reports Asia-Mediterranean capacity 49% above last year.

Timing decides the impact, Sogese notes. A sailing blanked in weeks 40 or 41 removes arrivals in Europe four to six weeks later, from late October to late November. Cargo produced before the holiday leaves in weeks 42 and 43 on full vessels, and a late booking risks rolling to week 44.

“The cargo held back by the holiday ships in weeks 42 and 43 and lands in Europe between mid-November and early December. Shippers who book those departures now will get space. Those who wait will roll.” said Andrea Monti, CEO & MD, Sogese.

SUEZ IS A NETWORK SHIFT WITH A SECURITY CONDITION

Sogese reads the Suez return as a network shift whose pace depends on security. On 14 September Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd moved Gemini services AE5, AE11, AE12 and ME2 back to Suez and said further changes depend on stability in the Red Sea area and no escalation of regional conflicts. Drewry counted 48 container transits in week 38, up from 41, and 68% above the same week of 2025 in week 39. On 8 October Drewry called a faster-than-expected return to Suez “the biggest threat to carrier efforts to support rates”.

“Suez is returning service by service, and each conversion takes one to two weeks off the voyage. That lowers freight immediately and helps cargo planning only where the receiving terminal is ready for earlier arrivals. Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd have made the return conditional on no escalation, so every plan needs a Cape-routing contingency.” said Andrea Monti, CEO & MD, Sogese.

THE MEDITERRANEAN PREMIUM HAS GONE, AND LIGURIAN PORTS ARE LAST IN THE QUEUE

Sogese notes that Genoa’s premium over Rotterdam on Drewry’s index has fallen from $1,530 on 9 July to $359 on 8 October. Xeneta puts the Far East to Mediterranean premium over North Europe at about $400 on 1 October, against $2,000 on 1 January. Sea-Intelligence data cited in the report show Gemini adding a net 22,402 TEU a week to Asia-Mediterranean.

Cheaper does not mean faster. On Maersk’s AE11, moved to Suez from 19 September, the rotation runs Shanghai, Yantian, Tanjung Pelepas, Suez, Tangier, Valencia, Barcelona, La Spezia, Genoa and Vado Ligure. Italian importers are the last discharge, so delay accumulated at earlier calls reaches them last, Sogese notes.

“If North Europe keeps falling, the Mediterranean follows. Importers should not fix Mediterranean rates beyond three months until weekly Suez transits stop rising.” said Andrea Monti, CEO & MD, Sogese.

WHAT SOGESE IS WATCHING: BLANK SAILINGS AFTER GOLDEN WEEK

Sogese’s base case is a further fall in rates through the fourth quarter, because Suez capacity is arriving faster than carriers can blank it. It reads a blank sailing count that stays at or below seven a week in weeks 43 and 44 as pointing to further declines, and a count well above it as pointing to a floor. Drewry counts six Asia-Europe blank sailings announced for next week, up from five, and the report notes its judgement that seven a week do not offset the Suez capacity returning. In Sogese’s scenario where Suez capacity outpaces demand, rates reach January levels: $2,763 for Shanghai to Rotterdam, 17% below the 8 October figure, and about $3,100 for Genoa, 16% below. Xeneta chief analyst Peter Sand said on 8 October that “we are not at the floor yet”.

“Unless blanks rise well above seven a week, Rotterdam’s January rate of $2,763 and Genoa near $3,100 are the next stops.” said Andrea Monti, CEO & MD, Sogese. Source: Sogese
takeaways: “Europe is entering the final quarter with two forces moving in opposite directions.
Capacity is becoming more available as Suez routings return, while carriers are simultaneously trying to protect utilisation through blank sailings.
For shippers, this means lower rates may offer an opportunity, but they should not be mistaken for a return to predictable service.

articles.title: Drewry: Cancelled Sailings Tracker Shows Capacity Gradually Returning
articles.summary: Our weekly tracker provides a snapshot of blank sailings announced by each Alliance versus the total number of scheduled sailings.
articles.body:
Our weekly tracker provides a snapshot of blank sailings announced by each Alliance versus the total number of scheduled sailings.

The post-Golden Week market is entering a new phase, with capacity gradually returning but pricing pressure building unevenly across the major trades.

Drewry’s World Container Index (WCI) stood at $4,351 per 40ft on 8 October, down 2% WoW, as rates eased across the Transpacific, Asia–Europe/Med and Transatlantic trades. Major pressure remains on Asia–Europe/Med, where the gradual return of services via Suez is adding effective capacity as carriers adjust to changing routing conditions.

Across the major East–West trades, 34 blank sailings are expected from week 42 (12–18 October) to week 46 (9–15 November) out of 713 planned sailings, representing a 5% cancellation rate, with 95% of scheduled sailings expected to operate. Disruptions are concentrated on Asia–North Europe/Med, accounting for 50% of cancellations, followed by the Transpacific eastbound at 32% and the Transatlantic at 18%.

For shippers, higher effective capacity and fewer cancellations could gradually ease supply pressure, although congestion and ongoing network adjustments may continue to constrain capacity and keep rates elevated on some trades.

In the next edition of Container Capacity Insight, we will continue to track changes in blank-sailing programmes, effective capacity, Suez routings and global port congestion as post-Golden Week operations settle. Source: Drewry

articles.title: Singapore LNG starts work on new jetty to boost LNG bunker supply
articles.summary: Terminal operator Singapore LNG (SLNG) has started construction of a third jetty at its Jurong Island terminal, which could increase its LNG bunkering capacity to 3 million mt/year.
articles.body:
Terminal operator Singapore LNG (SLNG) has started construction of a third jetty at its Jurong Island terminal, which could increase its LNG bunkering capacity to 3 million mt/year.

The new jetty is scheduled for completion in the second half of 2028 and will be capable of handling LNG carriers ranging from 5,800-80,000 cbm.

Unlike SLNG’s existing jetties, the new facility will be dedicated to small and mid-sized vessels, allowing the terminal to handle more LNG bunker reloads along with break-bulk operations.

Once operational, the jetty will be able to support around 2 million mt/year of LNG bunker reload demand. The total infrastructure will be able to handle up to 3 million mt/year.

“As demand for LNG bunkering continues to grow, Jetty 3 will strengthen Singapore’s ability to support the next phase of growth…” Leong Wei Hung, chief executive of SLNG said.

Separately, SLNG has secured ISCC EU certification for handling liquefied biomethane (LBM) at its terminal. The certification covers storage, regasification, bunkering and trucking operations, allowing customers to trace and account for certified LBM handled through the facility.

The new jetty will also be capable of handling LBM, giving SLNG additional flexibility to support demand for the lower-emission fuel. Source: By Konica Bhatt, ENGINE, https://www.engine.online/news/

articles.title: Dualog Launches Secure Messaging For Ship And Shore
articles.summary: Dualog has launched Dualog Chat, a secure messaging service built for shipping. The first service in Workspace by Dualog, Chat gives crews and shore teams a company-controlled space to communicate, with channels...
articles.body:
Dualog has launched Dualog Chat, a secure messaging service built for shipping. The first service in Workspace by Dualog, Chat gives crews and shore teams a company-controlled space to communicate, with channels organised by vessel, rank and role. Every user has a secure identity, with no shared logins.

Communication at sea is often fragmented. In a 2026 Dualog survey of 1,187 seafarers, 68% said important information is lost during crew handovers. Many rely on personal messaging apps to contact the office because there is no official channel available to the whole crew. Chat addresses this gap while running alongside the tools companies already use ashore.

For crew, Chat brings onboard and ship-to-shore communication into one place. Message histories stay with the role, giving officers signing on immediate access to the context they need. Shore teams can reach everyone in a particular rank across the fleet with a single message, or contact an individual directly. Users can exchange messages and voice notes and make audio and video calls over the connections available at sea.

For shore teams, operational conversations, sensitive information and the context behind decisions remain within a company-controlled platform. Details such as rates and port instructions are retained centrally, reducing reliance on personal messaging accounts.

Integration with crew management systems automatically updates access as crews rotate, reducing manual onboarding and offboarding. Fleets already using Dualog crew accounts can get started quickly. Individual user identities make communication traceable and support the unique identity and controlled access requirements set out by IMO and IACS.

“Dualog Chat connects people in a way that reflects how shipping operates,” said Silje Moan, Chief Commercial Officer at Dualog. “By organising communication around the vessel, the rank and the rotation, it helps crews retain context through each handover and shore teams reach the right person. The information that matters stays within the company.”

Chat is available on web, iOS and Android and is designed for maritime connectivity. Early access is open now. Further services planned for Workspace by Dualog include file sharing, maritime email and a native AI assistant. Source: Dualog

The first service in Workspace by Dualog, Chat gives crews and shore teams a company-controlled space to communicate, with channels organised by vessel, rank and role.

articles.title: Britain urges ships to prepare for life without reliable GPS
articles.summary: Britain has warned shipowners that satellite navigation can no longer be taken for granted in some of the world’s busiest shipping regions, urging crews to practise navigating without GPS as jamming and spoofing become...
articles.body:
Britain has warned shipowners that satellite navigation can no longer be taken for granted in some of the world’s busiest shipping regions, urging crews to practise navigating without GPS as jamming and spoofing become increasingly widespread.

In a new Marine Guidance Note, MGN 719, the UK’s Maritime and Coastguard Agency (MCA) warns that interference across the Baltic, Black Sea, Middle East Gulf and parts of East Asia means satellite-derived positioning, navigation and timing information can no longer be relied upon everywhere.

The warning extends well beyond electronic charts. The agency identifies a long list of potentially vulnerable equipment, including ECDIS, AIS, autopilots, dynamic positioning systems, radar, gyrocompasses and GMDSS communications equipment. Ashore, vessel traffic services, pilotage systems, port management platforms and automated logistics systems are also exposed.

The financial implications are considerable. Citing earlier UK government research, the MCA estimates that a seven-day GNSS outage could cost the British maritime economy £1.5bn ($2bn), including £1.3bn in port operations alone.

The guidance urges operators to identify precisely which systems depend on satellite-derived data, establish procedures for detecting interference and regularly drill crews in alternative navigation methods. Radar fixing, visual bearings, celestial navigation and dead reckoning are all recommended.

The notice follows growing evidence that satellite navigation interference is becoming a routine operational hazard rather than an occasional inconvenience in conflict zones.

Maritime intelligence firm Windward’s latest figures show an average of 5,131 GPS jamming incidents a day during the third quarter, with more than 124,000 individual vessels affected.

Research published earlier this year by the Royal Institute of Navigation found that 14% of survey respondents had experienced an unsafe or unlawful situation resulting from GNSS interference.

In July, SplashTech reported on a government questionnaire, believed to have originated in Britain, asking ship operators whether their crews had conducted GNSS-denial drills, understood the vulnerabilities of interconnected bridge equipment and could operate ECDIS in dead-reckoning mode.

More recently, SplashTech reported how four tankers in the Black Sea had apparently broadcast positions placing them in Lima, Peru, more than 12,000 km away. Separate monitoring identified 1,702 impossible position jumps involving 379 vessels in the Gulf of Oman over a single week in September.

The UK is investing in a terrestrial navigation backup through its enhanced Loran, or eLoran, programme, but the MCA’s latest guidance makes clear that technological alternatives will take time to become widely available.

Britain’s planned eLoran network is not expected to provide an initial timing capability until 2028, with full positioning and navigation services targeted for 2030.
takeaways: The warning extends well beyond electronic charts.
The agency identifies a long list of potentially vulnerable equipment, including ECDIS, AIS, autopilots, dynamic positioning systems, radar, gyrocompasses and GMDSS communications equipment.
Ashore, vessel traffic services, pilotage systems, port management platforms and automated logistics systems are also exposed.

Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe.

Moxie Media will host its first dedicated user event, Moxie Connect: User Conference 2026, a complimentary event open to all maritime professionals, on Wednesday, December 2, at the Ernest N. Morial Convention Center in New Orleans, alongside the International WorkBoat Show. The half-day event will bring together Moxie customers and professionals in maritime training, safety, compliance and workforce development for discussions, demonstrations and industry perspectives on the evolving role of technology in maritime learning.

Moxie Connect comes at an important point in Moxie Media’s evolution. In 2025, Moxie became part of Mintra, a global provider of digital learning and workforce management solutions. The combination brings together Moxie’s longstanding U.S. maritime training expertise, content and customer support with Mintra’s broader portfolio of learning technology, competency management and workforce solutions.

“For our customers, becoming part of Mintra has expanded what we can offer while allowing Moxie to continue doing what we do best in the U.S. maritime market,” said Martin Glenday, President of Moxie Media. “Moxie Connect is a chance to bring that expanded offering into one conversation and give customers and the broader maritime community a closer look at where training, technology and workforce management are headed.”

A key part of the expanded offering is Trainingportal, Mintra’s Learning and Competency Management System, which combines Moxie’s established approach to maritime learning with Mintra’s expanded capabilities for managing training, competency and compliance. Moxie Connect will allow customers and maritime organizations to see the platform in action, with demonstrations on user experience, mobile and offline learning capabilities, maritime training content and tools for managing workforce training.

The event will also explore the growing connection between training and competency management. Trainingportal includes capabilities that can help organizations establish role-based requirements, manage assessments and maintain evidence of competency alongside training records. The program will also introduce Mentor AI, Mintra’s AI solution, and discuss practical applications for using AI and digital learning tools to support continuous learning and workforce readiness.

“Technology is most useful when it helps organizations make better use of the information they already have about their people, their training and their requirements,” said Parker Hillery, Operations Manager and LMS Lead at Moxie Media. “The combination of competency management, training data and AI gives organizations new ways to understand workforce readiness while keeping the experience practical for the people responsible for training and compliance.”

Moxie Connect will also feature an Integration Partner Showcase, demonstrating how Trainingportal connects with vessel management systems to share training and competency information across an organization’s systems.

A regulatory update session will provide an industry perspective on current developments affecting maritime organizations. Additional sessions will address the future of Moxie’s maritime training content, including new and upcoming Coast Guard-related courses and other resources supporting maritime training and compliance.

The event is open to existing Moxie customers as well as maritime organizations interested in learning more about Moxie, Mintra and Trainingportal. Moxie Connect is free to attend, but space is limited and advance registration is required.

As an added benefit, registered attendees will receive a complimentary International WorkBoat Show exhibit hall pass, allowing participants to attend the morning event and then visit the WorkBoat exhibition.

A Southern-style breakfast, coffee and refreshments will be provided.

articles.title: Europe’s shore power deadline is racing ahead of the grid
articles.summary: Two EU regulations will require ports to provide shore power and ships to use it from 2030. But with grid upgrades taking up to a decade, the infrastructure needed to meet the deadline is struggling to keep pace. Alex...
articles.body:
Two EU regulations will require ports to provide shore power and ships to use it from 2030. But with grid upgrades taking up to a decade, the infrastructure needed to meet the deadline is struggling to keep pace. Alex Byelyavtsev reports.

By 2030 two EU rules meet at the quay. AFIR tells TEN-T core and comprehensive ports above a traffic threshold, not only the big hubs, to put shore power on the berth for 90% of qualifying container and passenger calls. FuelEU Maritime tells those ships, if they stay more than two hours, to connect and take their electrical load from it. One rule builds the socket. The other requires the ship to plug into it. The date, from Fit for 55, is already doing the ordering. It is not building the grid.

On the ship the box can be bought. In July 2026 Cavotec took an order to retrofit containerships with a containerised cable system while they stay in service. DNV had about 20% of world containerships equipped with a shore-power connection. Hapag-Lloyd is further along, about 35%. A company can fit a ship. FuelEU still names that company even when the quay has no live point, or a charter ship has no socket.

In the port the iron is thinner. Transport & Environment, from DNV, put guaranteed container connections at about 11% of what 31 European ports need by 2030. Much of the OPS already advertised is low voltage. Deepsea boxes need high voltage. The 90% test is still ahead of the cable.

The calendar does not match. From October 2026 to 31 December 2029 is a little over three years. ESPO, setting out the commission’s grid-connection guidance, puts extra grid build at four to ten years, against two to three for the port-side connection. If the request is not already in the queue, parts of the required build may not fit the time left. Rotterdam is aiming for the second half of 2028. ABB says that kit is meant to supply up to 32 containerships at once. The port’s own strategy still records grid congestion. Installed megawatts are not the event the grid sees. The event is coincidence. A 90% coverage test does not ask whether those megawatts are free at 07:00 on a Saturday.

The clock starts when the ship is alongside, not when the cable is live. Hamburg’s routine connection is about an hour to an hour and a half. If the commercial berth has no socket, the stay can still be a FuelEU call of more than two hours.

What a master can do is ask before arrival. Article 6 already lists the misses: no point, not enough power or grid stability, incompatibility on a certified ship installation, emergency. From 1 January 2035 those availability exceptions tighten to the lower of 10% of a ship’s annual calls or ten calls, unless the company shows it could not reasonably have known. That showing sits on the information exchanged before entry. A dead cabinet is a legal category. After 2035 an unasked miss can become a counted one, and a FuelEU penalty on the electricity that should have come from shore. That is not a hole found later. It is how a duty stays on the books when the connection cannot. IMO 2020 did not need that. A 0.50% fuel could be blended. A substation cannot.

The bill is separate. A parliament study759345) finds the EU can mandate the socket and still have no common price rule. Under the Energy Taxation Directive, electricity produced on board at berth must be exempt. Shore-side electricity is not covered by that exemption. A member state needs a Council authorisation to apply a reduced rate. Germany obtained one in June 2026, through 31 December 2029. In tramp trades the OPS invoice may not follow the bunker. The visible shore bill is still stacked against the auxiliary engines.

There is no sign of a general 2030 delay. If the megawatts, the berth and the cable are there, the auxiliaries stop. If they are not, the ship stays on its own plant and the call sits on the exception list. Article 6 already holds those misses. AFIR is due a review by 31 December 2026. A date that cannot be followed as written is then followed through exceptions, then through reviews. A date can mandate a connection. It cannot manufacture grid capacity. The plug is not the power.

articles.title: Connecting maritime digitalisation to process

While the technology needed to digitalise maritime operations is already here, much remains to be done to ensure organisations and their people are equipped to use it effectively, according to panellists at a recent Inmarsat Maritime ‘Connected to Perform’ seminar.

The maritime sector is awash with digital technology and data – but gaps still need to be bridged before stakeholders can extract maximum value from the tools available. This was the consensus among a panel of industry experts at a recent Inmarsat Maritime ‘Connected to Perform’ seminar in Hamburg.

The panel discussion, held during SMM Hamburg, explored how shipping can enable a digital, secure, and human-centric fleet – and how modern connectivity can support this objective.

Asked to identify the most significant gap between “what connectivity and technology can provide and what is being used by shipping companies”, Audra Drablos, Strategy Director at Inmarsat Maritime, argued that technology itself is no longer the issue.

“We’re connecting global fleets,” she said. “We’re using advanced analytics. We’re using preventative maintenance. So the technology, I think, is definitely there.” Instead, she indicated, the gap may lie in how organisations are using those technologies: “If we want to digitalise things, we also have to transform all the decision processes that we have.”

Drablos’s co-panellists outlined how their companies are using modern technology to digitalise their operations.

Patrick Briest, Senior Director of Operations for IT Products at Hapag-Lloyd, pointed to the container carrier’s adoption of real-time cargo tracking and voyage optimisation to maximise speed and flexibility. Konstantin Pohsin, Fleet Captain at Fairplay Towage, described the way predictive maintenance preserved operational readiness. And Matthias Becker, Managing Director of Anglo-Eastern Germany, highlighted the ship manager’s use of artificial intelligence to manage vessel emissions.

While these organisations have already implemented modern technology on a fleet-wide scale, their representatives nevertheless echoed Drablos’s point, with each identifying areas where further work is underway to optimise digital- and data-driven processes.

For Anglo-Eastern, the focus is on integrating disparate systems. “We get a lot of data today, and that’s in isolated systems and products,” said Becker, who added that the company could “uncover more savings and make better decisions when [it connects] all the different systems”.

In comparable remarks, Briest said Hapag-Lloyd had established its Fleet Data Ecosystem to bring all its data together so that it can “look at it holistically, interconnect it, and then drive the right insights out of it”. Referring back to Drablos’s comments, he continued: “Even if you have the dashboard – the tool that tells you what you should be doing – you have to change the way the whole organisation works, that processes work, that people work, to actually make it happen.”

At Fairplay Towage, the emphasis is on training to address what Pohsin called a “gap in knowledge” regarding connected onboard systems. “We have to investigate what is the proper way for educating all our employees in the application of these facilities,” he commented.

In Becker’s view, however, the industry can only achieve so much through training alone; managing the “complex challenge” of digital transformation will also depend on interdepartmental and cross-industry collaboration.

“Seafarers will not become IT experts,” he said. “Technicians remain technicians, and we have to bridge the gap in some way. So we have to bring together the crew, the offshore personnel, and the data analytics and IT side. We also need cooperation between operators, owners, managers, OEMs, and providers of IT systems.”

Supporting crews with the tools to perform their roles effectively was a recurring theme throughout the session. The purpose of technologies like AI, the panellists suggested, is not to replace human expertise – “don’t stop thinking with your own brain” was Pohsin’s message to seafarers – but to relieve personnel of time-consuming data-analysis and compliance-related tasks.

“I think that’s where AI could really help,” Drablos commented, pointing to a recent Seafarers Happiness Index report that revealed the seafarers with the lowest happiness scores are those with the most responsibility. “It could help in prioritising all that data and helping [seafarers] make better decisions,” she said.

Building on Drablos’s remarks, Briest added that AI could allow crews to focus on running their vessels, while an increasing use of cloud-based AI applications could drive greater demand for connectivity. “I believe the general connectivity requirement for these more intelligent, AI-driven systems is probably going to get bigger,” he said.

As the maritime industry’s “general connectivity requirement” grows, so too does the need for robust cyber-security solutions. Yet, as Drablos noted, “the question isn’t really about connectivity versus security. The question is how you can build security as your basis when you’re implementing your connectivity. I think that’s the important part: making it secure by design.”

articles.title: ABS, U.S. Energy Department Team Up on Nuclear-Powered Ships
articles.summary: Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe.

Photo caption (L to R): Ted Garrish, United States Assistant Secretary for Nuclear Energy, and John McDonald, ABS Chairman and CEO

The American Bureau of Shipping (ABS) and the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) have signed an agreement to advance the use of nuclear power in commercial shipping, including nuclear-powered vessels, floating power plants and the infrastructure needed to support them.

The memorandum of understanding, signed with DOE’s Office of Nuclear Energy, establishes a framework for joint work on advanced nuclear technologies and their potential maritime applications. The effort will also examine what would be required to develop a U.S. shipbuilding industry capable of constructing, operating and maintaining nuclear-powered vessels and offshore facilities.

Under the agreement, ABS and DOE will pursue concept and feasibility studies covering floating nuclear power systems and nuclear transportation corridors. The work will also address technical, regulatory, economic and policy challenges that have so far limited the commercial adoption of nuclear technology at sea.

“Advanced nuclear technology is moving from concept to application, and the maritime industry needs to be ready for it,” said ABS Chairman and CEO John McDonald.

“This agreement with DOE reflects the depth of work already underway and provides a framework to go further,” McDonald added.

ABS will also co-manage the Maritime Nuclear Applications Group (MNAG) and coordinate related work through the U.S. Maritime Administration’s U.S. Center for Maritime Innovation, where ABS serves as secretariat.

The agreement comes as interest in commercial maritime nuclear power continues to grow, driven by advances in smaller reactor designs that could make nuclear propulsion and floating power generation more practical.

While nuclear propulsion has been used aboard naval vessels for decades, its commercial adoption remains limited. Significant questions remain over reactor licensing, port access, liability, crew training and the regulatory responsibilities of flag and coastal states.

The U.S. government has stepped up efforts to address those barriers. In August, the Department of Energy hosted the launch of the International Atomic Energy Agency’s Atomic Technologies Licensed for Applications at Sea (ATLAS) initiative, aimed at developing an international framework for the safe and secure use of nuclear technology aboard ships and floating facilities.

ABS has also been expanding its work in the sector. The classification society has published rules for floating nuclear power plants and issued approvals in principle for several nuclear-powered vessel concepts, including a cargo ship propulsion system developed through an MIT-led maritime consortium .

Earlier this year, the U.S. Center for Maritime Innovation convened industry and government officials to examine regulatory barriers to deploying nuclear-powered ships and offshore energy platforms.

“Advanced nuclear technology has the potential to transform the commercial maritime industry and open new markets for American innovation,” said Assistant Secretary for Nuclear Energy Ted Garrish.

Garrish said the partnership would draw on decades of U.S. nuclear experience to examine how next-generation reactors could be safely introduced into commercial maritime operations.

The new agreement does not announce a specific vessel construction project or deployment schedule. Instead, it expands cooperation between the federal government and ABS as the industry works toward making commercial nuclear power at sea technically and economically viable.

articles.title: Hambantota port reaches TEU milestone
articles.summary: Hambantota International Port has surpassed one million TEUs in cumulative container throughput since the commissioning of new quay cranes in 2025, marking a significant milestone in the rapid growth of its container...
articles.body:
Hambantota International Port has surpassed one million TEUs in cumulative container throughput since the commissioning of new quay cranes in 2025, marking a significant milestone in the rapid growth of its container operations.

The port handled 428,036 TEUs in 2025 and 574,196 TEUs year-to-date in 2026, bringing combined volume to 1,002,232 TEUs.

MSC, HIP’s principal container customer, has contributed significantly to the growth trajectory. In April 2026, the MSC Marie Leslie set a new single-vessel handling record of 7,968 container moves, equivalent to 13,260 TEUs, during a single call.

HIP subsequently achieved its highest-ever monthly throughput of 80,325 TEUs in June, reflecting operational preparedness and available capacity during a period of uncertainty affecting major global trade routes.

To support sustained growth toward a long-term target of two million TEUs annual capacity, HIP is undertaking a US$ 108 million expansion programme encompassing six new quay cranes and 16 rubber-tyred gantry cranes, expected to be commissioned by the end of February 2027.

Once operational, the new equipment will strengthen ship-to-shore and yard-handling capacity, support utilisation of an additional 1,300 metres of berth space and take total container quay length to nearly two kilometres.

The container yard will be expanded by 30% to accommodate rising throughput, and reefer capacity will also be increased.

HIPG CEO Wilson Qu described the one million TEU milestone as a strong indication of customer confidence built through close shipping line engagement, operational reliability and responsiveness to changing requirements.

Chief Operations Officer Tommy Yang characterised the investment strategy as focused on developing capacity ahead of demand while maintaining operational efficiency and financial sustainability, creating the scale required to achieve the two million TEU target.

articles.title: New Reports Reveal Five More Ships Hit Near Hormuz
articles.summary: Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe.
articles.body:
Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe.

Vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman, July 31, 2026. REUTERS/Stringer

Five more commercial vessels were struck in and around the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday, including a containership and four tankers, as attacks on merchant shipping continue to escalate across the region.

UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) disclosed four of the incidents in time-late reports on Monday, adding to an already growing number of attacks reported in recent weeks. Four vessels were struck while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, while a fifth tanker was hit by a drone near Sohar anchorage, Oman.

The latest reports include an outbound product tanker, an outbound crude oil tanker, another outbound tanker and a container ship transiting inbound through the strait. All four were struck by unidentified projectiles, according to UKMTO.

In one incident, UKMTO confirmed that the crew of an outbound tanker was safe, although the environmental impact remained unknown. The other reports provided no details on casualties or the extent of damage.

The fifth incident involved a tanker near Sohar anchorage that was struck by an uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV). UKMTO initially classified the incident as suspicious activity before upgrading it to an attack. Local authorities were assisting with the evacuation of the crew, while damage and environmental assessments remained incomplete.

The reports follow a particularly violent weekend for commercial shipping in the region, including earlier attacks on tankers in Hormuz and a U.S. military strike that disabled a commercial cargo vessel in the Gulf of Oman.

The new incidents also follow the release of the Joint Maritime Information Center’s October 11 advisory , which classified the security threat in the Strait of Hormuz as SEVERE , its second-highest threat category.

That assessment, covering incidents confirmed through approximately 1500 UTC Sunday, had already identified three recent tanker attacks in the strait, including one reported late. It warned that further deliberate attacks were highly likely and cited continued harassment, surveillance and pressure on commercial vessels by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

The advisory also highlighted an expanding geographic threat, with attacks no longer confined to vessels passing through the strait itself. Recent strikes have targeted ships anchored off the United Arab Emirates and vessels operating elsewhere inside the Persian Gulf.

The widening pattern of attacks comes as commercial traffic through Hormuz remains sharply reduced despite U.S. efforts to restore shipping flows.

According to JMIC, U.S. Naval Cooperation and Guidance for Shipping (NCAGS) figures showed approximately 29 vessel transits per day over the 72 hours ending October 10, compared with a historical average of roughly 138 per day. Independent tracking data indicated substantially fewer transits, reflecting differences in reporting and methodology.

The continuing attacks raise further questions about the sustainability of any recovery in commercial shipping through the strait.

They also underscore the limitations of official incident counts. With multiple attacks reported after the fact, even the most recent security assessments may not fully reflect conditions facing merchant vessels and their crews.

UKMTO has urged ships to transit with caution and report suspicious activity as authorities investigate the latest incidents.

articles.title: Cameroon, Georgia Receive FMS for Metal Shark Patrol Boats
articles.summary: Louisiana-based boatbuilder Metal Shark has been awarded two U.S. Coast Guard Foreign Military Sales (FMS) contracts to produce patrol boats for the maritime forces of Cameroon and the Republic of Georgia. Each...
articles.body:
Louisiana-based boatbuilder Metal Shark has been awarded two U.S. Coast Guard Foreign Military Sales (FMS) contracts to produce patrol boats for the maritime forces of Cameroon and the Republic of Georgia. Each contract includes a Metal Shark 38 Defiant patrol boat, transport trailer, spare-parts package, and operator training. The vessels will be constructed at Metal Shark's production facility in Jeanerette, Louisiana.

The welded-aluminum 38 Defiant is a military and law-enforcement patrol platform designed to support coastal patrol, maritime interdiction, port security, search and rescue, and other security missions. Metal Shark's 38 Defiant platform is operated by U.S. partner nations across Africa, Asia, the Caribbean, Europe, Latin America and the Middle East.

The vessel combines high-speed performance and maneuverability with Metal Shark's Defiant-series pilothouse, which provides enhanced visibility and all-weather crew protection. The adaptable platform may be configured with multiple propulsion arrangements and mission-specific equipment to meet a broad range of mission profiles.

Through the U.S. Foreign Military Sales program, the vessels and associated support packages will help Cameroon and Georgia strengthen their maritime law-enforcement capabilities, protect territorial waters and critical infrastructure, and respond more effectively to evolving regional security challenges.

articles.title: Soaring Tanker Rates Leave Americas Awash in Crude Oil
articles.summary: Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe.
articles.body:
Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe.

By Georgina McCartney and Arathy Somasekhar

HOUSTON, Oct 12 (Reuters) – Dense heavy crude, which oil refiners around the world favor for its typically low cost, is piling up in the Americas as soaring freight rates have stifled exports and US refiners have been running close to their limits.

The glut in North and South America has opened an unusual split in the global oil market, as buyers in Asia and Europe struggle with supply shortages and benchmark prices hold above $100 a barrel.

Heavy crude is a denser type of oil that Asian, many US, and some European refineries are typically configured to process. It is usually cheaper than light crude, offering refiners better margins, when shipping costs are affordable.

“It’s all freight,” said Scott Shelton, an energy specialist at TP ICAP. Venezuela, the US and Canada all produce more oil than they consume, he said, so they rely on exports to Asia to balance their crude markets.

With US diesel prices soaring, the cheap, stranded barrels should be getting snapped up in a diesel-starved market, since heavy crude yields more of the fuel than lighter grades. But Gulf Coast refiners have already bought as much as they can process, analysts and traders said.

Venezuelan exports have surged since the US captured former President Nicolas Maduro in January, then started pushing to reactivate the country’s oil sector. Canadian output is at a record and Washington has released more than 130 million barrels from its emergency reserve.

The cost of hiring a supertanker from the US Gulf Coast to Asia, meanwhile, has more than quintupled since February, as ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman tie up vessels worldwide.

“You need a ship and the price of ships are going up, and the availability ships are going down,” Shelton said.

Flagship Canadian, Colombian and Ecuadorian heavy crude grades have all eased more than $10a barrel to trade at their lowest level in six weeks, according to price reporting agency Argus Media. Prices for Western Canada Select, excluding shipping or insurance costs, was around $74 on Thursday; Colombia’s main grade Vasconia was trading at around $84; and Ecuador’s Oriente was trading at around $76, Argus said.

Venezuelan crude excluding shipping costs was trading around $74.50 a barrel on Thursday, two traders said.

Shipping oil on a supertanker from the US Gulf Coast to Europe was estimated to cost around $46 million, or $24.50 a barrel, last week, including ship-to-ship transfer and other costs, according to Georgios Sakellariou, a Signal Maritime analyst. That compares with $6.5 million or around $4 a barrel before the Iran war broke out in late February.

The cost of a tanker from the Americas to Asia rose to more than $80 million, or about $40 a barrel, last week compared with around $10-15 million near the start of the year.

US refineries have operated at about 93.5% capacity on an average weekly basis so far this year, according to the Energy Information Administration. That is the highest level in 28 years as they crank out as much as fuel as they can to profit from record high diesel prices. While those refineries are complex and geared to run a heavier crude slate, they can only process it up to a certain percentage of their total capacity.

“While Venezuela and US emergency barrels have been a factor for months now, leading to near maximum US coker utilization, high freight is now a further headwind to shipping these barrels east and is forcing heavy sour storage builds in the Americas,” Irwin added. Cokers convert residual crude oil into feedstocks for diesel and gasoline production, and a heavier crude slate requires them to run at a higher capacity.

Many US refineries are also configured for offshore Gulf of Mexico crude such as Mars Sour, rather than Canadian or Venezuelan oil that must be mixed with lighter feedstock.

(Reporting by Georgina McCartney and Arathy Somasekhar in Houston, Amanda Stephenson in Calgary; Editing by Liz Hampton and Nathan Crooks and David Gregorio)

articles.title: Stena Bulk Registers Fourth and Fifth Vessels Under the Swedish Flag
articles.summary: Counsellor Thomas Dahlman of the Swedish Embassy in China (left) and Steve Targett, Master of Stena Superior (right). © Stena Bulk
articles.body:
Counsellor Thomas Dahlman of the Swedish Embassy in China (left) and Steve Targett, Master of Stena Superior (right). © Stena Bulk

Tanker shipping company Stena Bulk announced that Stena Imperator has been officially registered under the Swedish flag. This follows the reflagging of the Suezmax tanker Stena Superior in Shenzhen, China, last month.

These are the fourth and fifth reflaggings completed under the program Stena Bulk announced in July 2025 to bring vessels into the Swedish Register of Shipping.

Stena Imperator's reflagging was completed yesterday in San Francisco. The 49,690 dwt product and chemical tanker was built by Guangzhou Shipbuilding International (GSI) and delivered in 2017. It is the first vessel of Stena Bulk's IMOIIMAX design to join the programme.

When Stena Bulk announced the program, Sweden had no large tankers on its national ship register. The program was designed to strengthen Sweden's maritime sector and its competitiveness as a flag state, support the country's national preparedness and strategic resilience, and create opportunities for Swedish seafarers. It followed recent reforms that have made the Swedish register more competitive, including the removal of stamp duty, a competitive tonnage tax and an improved Ship Register.

Large plume of black smoke rises from the fuel storage area at King Khalid International Airport, in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, September 19, 2026. Picture taken with a mobile phone. REUTERS/Stringer

(Bloomberg) — This weekend’s deadly attacks on Riyadh’s main airport have demonstrated the ability of Yemen’s Houthis to strike at the heart of Saudi power, raising the risk of a dangerous escalation that could draw in the US.

Saturday’s strike killed 12 people and wounded 309, while an attack on Sunday killed one person and injured 11. The Houthis swiftly claimed the attacks, saying they were a response to “Saudi aggression,” including a strike on the airport in the Yemeni capital of Sanaa.

Saudi fighter jets are already backing a counteroffensive by Yemeni government forces after the Houthis seized territory near Bab el-Mandeb, a critical chokepoint for global shipping at the southern entrance to the Red Sea.

The Houthis had largely stayed on the sidelines after the US-Israeli war against Iran began in February. But the latest offensive illustrates how the group — a member of Iran’s so-called axis of resistance — has developed into its own autonomous fighting force, with its own sophisticated weapons supply chain and an ability to operate and escalate as they see fit, at times in coordination with the Islamic Republic.

Despite the airport strikes and fresh tanker attacks around the Strait of Hormuz, oil dropped on Monday. Traders instead weighed President Donald Trump’s claim of an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine, with Brent crude slipping below $104 a barrel after a two-day gain.

The attacks put de facto ruler Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman under mounting pressure to escalate a war the country has spent years trying to escape, against an opponent that’s arguably more capable than it’s ever been. They also present difficult choices for the US and the kingdom’s new defense partners, Turkey and Pakistan, over how far to go in helping Saudi Arabia respond.

“By escalating their attacks, they are trying to pressure Saudi Arabia into stepping back and halting its air campaign,” said Ahmed Nagi, the International Crisis Group’s senior analyst for Yemen. “Riyadh sees these strikes as a serious escalation, particularly given their unprecedented nature, and is likely to respond with greater military pressure.”

With an American among those killed on Saturday, Trump also faces growing pressure to act. Asked on Saturday whether the US would join strikes against the Houthis, he said: “We may. We’re going to look at it.”

“Riyadh will want direct US strikes against the Houthis, air defense capabilities, increased intelligence sharing, and political cover for an intensified campaign in Yemen,” said William Usher, a former senior Middle East analyst at the Central Intelligence Agency.

The Saudi-led coalition blamed the Houthis for Saturday’s attack, calling it “a full-fledged war crime.”

Saudi Arabia led a coalition that intervened in Yemen in 2015 to restore the internationally recognized government, only to spend years bombing the Houthis without dislodging them. A UN-brokered truce in 2022 sharply reduced the fighting and offered Riyadh a way to wind down its involvement while the militant group’s capabilities and reach grew.

Saudi Arabia’s Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan and his Iranian counterpart Abbas Araghchi discussed the latest escalation in the region in a phone call, according to a report Sunday by the state-run Saudi Press Agency.

Saudi Arabia has spent billions of dollars building one of the region’s most sophisticated militaries, equipped with American F-15 fighter jets and Patriot missile defenses whose interceptors cost as much as $5 million apiece. Yet repeated strikes have shuttered the international airport serving its capital, grounding hundreds of flights and forcing schools to move online.

The attacks may be a sign of the pressure the Houthis are facing in Yemen. After the group seized the Red Sea port of Mokha and territory near Bab el-Mandeb last month, Yemeni government forces launched a counteroffensive backed by Saudi warplanes. The coalition says it has recaptured Mokha and destroyed scores of Houthi military targets.Play Video

“The Houthis are feeling the impact of the Saudi airstrikes carried out over the past few days in areas under their control,” Nagi said. “They have lost a significant number of fighters, and several strategic sites have been hit, including drone workshops, arms depots and telecommunications towers.”

Still, the Houthis retain an arsenal of Iranian-designed ballistic missiles capable of reaching Riyadh and cheap attack drones that can be assembled locally. The group has survived years of Saudi and US bombing campaigns, and the latest strikes demonstrate how difficult it may be to stop it from inflicting further damage on the kingdom.

articles.title: Steerprop Secures Propulsion Contract for Danish Multi-Role Environmental Vessels
articles.summary: Three new Multi-Role Environmental vessels being built by Hvide Sande Shipyard for the Royal Danish Navy, will feature twin CRP azimuth propulsors, tunnel thruster, permanent-magnet motors and integrated propulsion and...
articles.body:
Three new Multi-Role Environmental vessels being built by Hvide Sande Shipyard for the Royal Danish Navy, will feature twin CRP azimuth propulsors, tunnel thruster, permanent-magnet motors and integrated propulsion and brigde controls supplied by Steerprop. Credit: Steerprop

Finnish marine propulsion provider Steerprop has secured a contract with Hvide Sande Shipyard to supply complete propulsion packages for three Multi-Role Environmental Vessels being built for the Royal Danish Navy.

The vessels have been commissioned by the Danish Ministry of Defence Acquisition and Logistics Organisation and are being built by Orlogsskibe Danmark, a Danish consortium comprising OSK Design, Karstensens Skibsværft and Hvide Sande Shipyard. The hulls are under construction at Karstensens Skibsværft's yard in Gdańsk, Poland, before being transferred to Hvide Sande Shipyard in Denmark for final outfitting, commissioning and sea trials. Steerprop's contract is with Hvide Sande Shipyard.

Each vessel will be equipped with two Steerprop Contra-Rotating Propeller (CRP) azimuth propulsors, each rated at 1,400 kW, with Steerprop also delivering the thrusters’ permanent-magnet motors. The full Steerprop scope of supply also includes third-party tunnel thrusters, bridge control systems and the complete propulsion control system, providing an integrated propulsion package designed to support the vessels' DNV Ice Class 1C requirements. Steerprop will also supply bridge controls and the propulsion control system, compliant with DNV's SP2 cyber security requirements.

Steerprop's Contra-Rotating Propeller technology uses two propellers rotating in opposite directions on a single shaft, increasing net thrust by 10–17% compared with conventionally powered single-propeller systems. In demanding ice conditions, the design has demonstrated approximately 10% lower ice resistance, up to 50% higher speed in brash ice and significantly faster ridge penetration, enabling vessels to maintain operational capability in challenging environments while improving overall efficiency.

Construction of the first vessel is already underway at Karstensens Skibsværft's yard in Gdańsk. Steerprop will begin deliveries of the propulsion packages in March 2027, with final outfitting taking place at Hvide Sande Shipyard in Denmark. The first vessel is expected to enter service in 2029.

articles.title: GEODIS expands defence logistics capabilities in Poland
articles.summary: GEODIS has obtained a new certification in Poland, enabling the logistics company to provide specialized transport services for the defence sector, including the handling of strategically important goods and dual-use...
articles.body:
GEODIS has obtained a new certification in Poland, enabling the logistics company to provide specialized transport services for the defence sector, including the handling of strategically important goods and dual-use products.

The company secured the Internal Compliance Programmes (ICP) certificate, which confirms that its internal procedures meet specific security and regulatory compliance requirements.

The certification expands GEODIS’ capabilities in Poland, allowing it to serve customers whose shipments are subject to strict national and European Union regulations.

These include companies transporting goods, technologies and services classified as strategically important, as well as products with both civilian and military applications.

The certificate was issued by CCJ, an accredited certification body operating within the Military University of Technology in Poland.

To obtain the certification, GEODIS reviewed and updated its internal procedures, conducted audits, trained employees and established responsibilities for its internal control system.

The system will remain subject to ongoing supervision and periodic assessments.

“This is another step in the development of specialist services of GEODIS in Poland,” said Marc Vollet, EVP of European Road Network at GEODIS.

The certification also supports the company’s ability to work with customers requiring additional safeguards for supply chain security, information access and regulatory compliance.

With the certification in place, GEODIS can pursue additional opportunities in Poland’s specialized logistics market, particularly among businesses operating in regulated sectors.

The development forms part of the company’s broader strategy to strengthen its transport services while maintaining security and compliance standards.

However, GEODIS has not announced any new defence transport contracts, fleet investments or additional facilities in connection with the certification.

The announcement therefore marks an expansion of the company’s service capabilities rather than the launch of a specific logistics project.

articles.title: EU Targets Major Russian Shipyards in Sweeping Sanctions Expansion
articles.summary: Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe.
articles.body:
Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe.

Smoke rises from a civilian vessel on fire, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in Odesa, Ukraine July 19, 2026.Picture taken with a mobile phone. REUTERS/Stringer

The European Union has imposed sanctions on some of Russia’s most important shipyards, including major submarine builders, naval ship-repair facilities and yards involved in commercial vessel construction, as part of a sweeping expansion of restrictions targeting the country’s military-industrial complex.

The new sanctions , adopted Monday, add 826 Russian companies and 743 executives to the EU’s sanctions list. The measures represent the largest single expansion of the bloc’s sanctions listings since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Among the companies named are Admiralty Shipyards in St. Petersburg, Sevmash in Severodvinsk, Amur Shipbuilding Plant in Russia’s Far East, and Severnaya Verf, another major St. Petersburg shipyard.

The designations also include Zvezdochka Ship Repair Center, a major facility for submarine maintenance and modernization, and Dalzavod Ship Repair Center in Vladivostok, which supports Russia’s Pacific Fleet.

The sanctions reach beyond Russia’s principal naval shipyards. Vyborg Shipyard, Sredne-Nevsky Shipyard, Nevsky Shipbuilding and Ship Repair Plant, and Vympel Shipbuilding Plant are also included, extending the restrictions to facilities involved in both military and civilian vessel construction.

Several other ship-repair facilities, including the 13th Ship Repair Plant in Sevastopol and the 33rd and 82nd ship-repair plants, are also among the newly designated entities.

The breadth of the listings is notable for Russia’s shipbuilding industry, where several major yards serve both military and commercial markets.

Sevmash is central to Russia’s nuclear submarine construction program, while Admiralty Shipyards builds conventional submarines. Severnaya Verf is involved in the construction of naval surface combatants, and Amur Shipbuilding Plant builds vessels for Russia’s Pacific Fleet.

Vyborg Shipyard, meanwhile, has been involved in the construction of icebreakers and offshore vessels, while Nevsky Shipbuilding and Ship Repair Plant has built commercial vessels as well as ships for government customers.

The sanctions impose asset freezes and prohibit EU persons and companies from making funds or economic resources available to the designated entities. They do not, by themselves, constitute a blanket prohibition on Russian-built vessels or commercial ships constructed at the affected yards.

According to the EU’s implementing regulation , the companies were identified by the Russian government as belonging to its military-industrial complex and eligible for federal subsidies supporting employee housing costs.

The EU cited those links as grounds for the designations.

The shipbuilding measures form one part of a much larger sanctions expansion focused heavily on Russia’s weapons production capacity. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said more than half of the nearly 1,600 new listings are connected to the production chain for ballistic missiles.

“This is the single largest expansion of our sanctions list since Russia started its war,” Kallas said.

“We are making it significantly harder, slower and more expensive for Russia to produce the weapons it uses to kill Ukrainians.”

The latest measures are distinct from the EU’s sanctions targeting Russia’s shadow fleet, which have focused on vessels involved in transporting Russian oil and circumventing Western restrictions.

articles.title: Construction of wind turbines has begun at Port of Zeebrugge
articles.summary: Preparatory groundworks have commenced this month for the construction of eight new wind turbines in the port of Zeebrugge, with a total capacity of 42.6 MW, in a joint investment by ENGIE, Port of Antwerp-Bruges and...
articles.body:
Preparatory groundworks have commenced this month for the construction of eight new wind turbines in the port of Zeebrugge, with a total capacity of 42.6 MW, in a joint investment by ENGIE, Port of Antwerp-Bruges and Portfineco, a vehicle jointly owned by Zefier and Port of Antwerp-Bruges.

ENGIE will manage the operational management of the turbines through the joint venture company Seagull I.

Three of the eight turbines will be located on the premises of the Wallenius Wilhelmsen RoRo terminal, with the remaining five sited on the premises of International Car Operators, where ENGIE, ICO and Portfineco already commissioned an 11-turbine wind farm of 44 MW capacity in 2020.

Tower masts, nacelles and blades are scheduled for installation in the second half of 2027, with the turbines expected to begin generating approximately 115 gigawatt-hours of renewable electricity annually from the start of 2028, equivalent to the average consumption of approximately 33,000 Belgian households.

Vincent Verbeke, CEO of ENGIE Belgium, described the project as part of the company’s focus on large-scale renewable development in port and industrial areas, strengthening Zeebrugge’s role as an energy hub for the region.

Dirk De fauw, Vice-Chairman of Port of Antwerp-Bruges and Mayor of Bruges, noted that the project brings the port well on its way to reaching half a gigawatt of installed wind capacity across its platforms by 2030.

Henk Kindt, Chairman of Zefier, highlighted Portfineco’s participation as reflecting the cooperative’s commitment to renewable energy benefiting its 160 shareholder municipalities.

articles.title: Paris Wheat Rises As Algerian Purchases Tender, Hope of Black Sea Peace Fades
articles.summary: European wheat futures in Paris rose on Monday, recovering from a sharp fall on Friday, as big importer Algeria issued a wheat purchase tender and hopes for a Black Sea peace deal faded.
articles.body:
European wheat futures in Paris rose on Monday, recovering from a sharp fall on Friday, as big importer Algeria issued a wheat purchase tender and hopes for a Black Sea peace deal faded.

Export-boosting euro weakness also supported.

Benchmark December milling wheat on the Paris-based Euronext exchange rose 0.3% to €242.75 ($271.15) a metric ton at 1534 GMT.

Algeria's state grains agency OAIC issued an international tender to buy milling wheat closing on Tuesday. The tender as usual indicated a nominal 50,000 metric tons, but Algeria, one of the world's largest wheat importers, often buys considerably more in its tenders.

"You've got the OAIC tender, the euro-dollar rate and Russia-Ukraine attacks continuing," a futures broker said.

Traders hoped the Algerian tender could remove several hundred thousand tons of supplies from the wheat market. The country bought about 500,000 tons in its last tender on September 15, but the impact was blunted as it was believed French wheat would again be excluded from the tender because of political tension between France and Algeria.

Price support also came from fading hopes of progress towards any Black Sea peace deal that would allow Russia and Ukraine to resume ship-borne exports.

US President Donald Trump announced a Ukrainian-Russian energy ceasefire on Sunday, initially sparking hopes for progress in resuming shipborne Black Sea wheat exports from Russia and Ukraine, which stalled after recent attacks.

But Russia hit at least six energy targets during a night and morning of airstrikes across Ukraine, President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Monday, adding this showed Moscow had no interest in any energy ceasefire.

“The Trump energy ceasefire announcement did generate some hope of some progress towards Black Sea peace negotiations but reaction from both sides was tepid and hopes have faded," a German trader added.

articles.title: TT Club and UK P&I Club secure member approval for merger
articles.summary: TT Club and UK P&I Club have secured approval from their members for a proposed merger that will bring together two major insurance organisations serving the global maritime, container and logistics industries.
articles.body:
TT Club and UK P&I Club have secured approval from their members for a proposed merger that will bring together two major insurance organisations serving the global maritime, container and logistics industries.

The decision was confirmed following separate Special General Meetings held on 7 and 8 October 2026. The merger is scheduled to take effect on 20 February 2027, subject to the necessary regulatory approvals.

The combined organisation will operate under a new parent company, United Transport Mutual Limited (UTM), with annual premium income of approximately US$750 million and free reserves of around US$888 million.

The merger will bring together the UK P&I Club’s marine insurance operations and TT Club’s activities across container transport, ports, terminals and logistics.

According to the organisations, UK P&I Club insures more than 250 million tonnes of owned and chartered shipping tonnage, while TT Club provides insurance coverage for 80% of the world’s container fleet.

TT Club also has an insurable interest in more than 70 of the world’s 100 largest ports, giving the proposed group a substantial presence across maritime transport and cargo handling operations.

The two organisations expect the combination to strengthen their financial resources and expand access to specialist expertise in underwriting, claims management and loss prevention.

The merger is also expected to generate an overall 5% improvement in the combined ratio, a key measure of underwriting performance.

Despite the integration, both clubs will retain their existing names, brands and market positions. Their members will continue to be served by their respective underwriting, claims and service teams.

United Transport Mutual will serve as the parent company, overseeing group governance, capital management, regulatory compliance and shared operational functions.

The new structure will allow TT Club and UK P&I Club to maintain their individual insurance products and underwriting approaches while operating within a broader mutual insurance group.

UTM is also expected to become the parent entity for the acquisition of Thomas Miller Holdings, the insurance management business associated with the clubs.

Thomas Miller’s shareholders have accepted the joint acquisition offer, although the transaction remains subject to regulatory approval.

The organisations said the proposed acquisition would bring the management business under mutual ownership as part of the wider restructuring.

Niels Smedegaard has been appointed Chairman of United Transport Mutual, with Morten Engelstoft and Jan Valkier serving as co-Chairs.

Andrew Taylor will become Chief Executive Officer of UTM, while William Beveridge will succeed him as Chief Executive Officer of UK P&I Club. Kevin King will remain Chief Executive Officer of TT Club.

The leadership changes will take effect through a phased transition as the merger progresses.

Morten Engelstoft, Chairman of TT Club, said the combination reflects the increasingly interconnected risks facing shipping, ports, terminals and logistics businesses.

The organisations confirmed that existing arrangements with members, brokers and clients will remain unchanged during the transition.

The merger remains subject to regulatory approvals before its planned completion in February 2027.
takeaways: TT Club and UK P&I Club have secured approval from their members for a proposed merger that will bring together two major insurance organisations serving the global maritime, container and logistics industries.
The decision was confirmed following separate Special General Meetings held on 7 and 8 October 2026.
The merger is scheduled to take effect on 20 February 2027, subject to the necessary regulatory approvals.
