articles.title: Port of Los Angeles sets monthly cargo record
articles.summary: The Port of Los Angeles handled 1,042,652 TEUs in September 2026, the busiest month in the port’s 118-year history, surpassing the previous monthly record set in July 2025 by more than 20,000 units.
articles.body:
The Port of Los Angeles handled 1,042,652 TEUs in September 2026, the busiest month in the port’s 118-year history, surpassing the previous monthly record set in July 2025 by more than 20,000 units.

The record month capped the busiest quarter in port history, with nearly 3 million TEUs handled from July through September, while the four-month stretch from June through September produced nearly 4 million TEUs, also the strongest such period on record.

Loaded imports reached 545,696 TEUs in September, up 19% year-on-year, while loaded exports totalled 125,751 TEUs, up 10%. Empty containers reached approximately 371,206 TEUs, the highest monthly total in port history.

Through the first nine months of 2026, the port has handled nearly 8.1 million TEUs, more than 3% ahead of the same period last year.

Executive Director Gene Seroka attributed the record performance to resilient consumer demand, inventory replenishment by importers, and cargo allocation shifting toward Los Angeles as shippers navigate challenges along Suez Canal and Panama Canal routes.

He also noted that tariffs are lower than levels seen earlier in the year, giving importers greater cost certainty.

Harvard Business School Professor Willy Shih, joining the monthly media briefing, described a broader shift in corporate supply chain strategy from pure cost optimisation toward flexibility in sourcing, manufacturing and cargo routing amid continued global trade uncertainty.

Mayor Karen Bass credited the port’s waterfront workforce, the ILWU and Executive Director Seroka for the historic result, describing the port as an extraordinary economic engine supporting good-paying union jobs and maintaining Los Angeles’s status as a global trade and commerce competitor.
takeaways: The Port of Los Angeles handled 1,042,652 TEUs in September 2026, the busiest month in the port’s 118-year history, surpassing the previous monthly record set in July 2025 by more than 20,000 units.

articles.title: Port of Gothenburg Quay Reinforcement Completed Successfully
articles.summary: The container terminal at the Port of Gothenburg. Photo: Port of Gothenburg.
articles.body:
The container terminal at the Port of Gothenburg. Photo: Port of Gothenburg.

Following more than two years of extensive work, the reinforcement of the south quay at the container terminal at the Port of Gothenburg has been completed on schedule and within budget. The Skandia Gateway project will now enter its next major phase, with blasting and dredging works closest to the quay commencing on October 13.

Since spring 2024, NCC has carried out reinforcement works along the westernmost 700 meters of the container terminal’s south quay. The quay reinforcement is a central part of Skandia Gateway and is essential to deepening the area closest to the quay, enabling larger container vessels with deeper draughts to call at the port from the turn of 2028/2029.

More than 200,000 cubic meters of soft dredged material and approximately 30,000 cubic meters of rock will be removed. The area closest to the quay is being designed to accommodate vessels with a maximum draught of 17.5 meters. The works are expected to be completed in March 2027.

The work has now been completed on schedule and within the budget set for the contract.

In parallel, the Swedish Maritime Administration is procuring the more extensive blasting and dredging works in the fairway and turning basin, as well as modifications to the navigational aids. The Swedish Maritime Administration plans to sign a contract for this part of the project in early 2027.

Skandia Gateway is being designed to accommodate container vessels up to 430 meters long and 65 meters wide. These vessels will be 30 meters longer and five meters wider, with draughts of up to four meters deeper than those currently calling at the container terminal.

Work in the fairway and turning basin is scheduled to begin in August 2027. The shared ambition of the Port of Gothenburg and the Swedish Maritime Administration is for the new fairway and quay to become operational before the end of 2028.

Lloyd’s Register (LR) and Sagar Defence Engineering Limited (SDEL) have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to help create practical pathways for the safe certification, assurance and regulatory acceptance of autonomous and remotely operated maritime systems.

As interest in autonomous technologies and remotely operated systems grows across commercial, government and defense sectors, developers and operators face increasing pressure to demonstrate that new systems can operate safely, reliably and in line with evolving regulatory requirements.

LR and Sagar Defence will work together to bridge the gap between technological innovation and operational deployment, helping move autonomous maritime systems from concept to approved operation.

The MoU combines LR's expertise in classification, assurance and regulatory compliance with Sagar Defence's experience developing autonomous and remotely operated platforms. The partnership will focus on supporting the classification, certification and operational acceptance of autonomous systems while helping shape the rules, guidance and assurance frameworks needed for wider industry adoption.

The two organizations will work together to develop practical approaches to verification, validation and testing, alongside classification readiness assessments and assurance methodologies.

The collaboration will also support the development of operational concepts, mission profiles and safety cases, while enabling closer engagement with regulators, government agencies and industry stakeholders to support the evolution of certification pathways for autonomous technologies.

articles.summary: Global container freight rates remained under pressure in the latest weekly readings, with several major benchmarks declining around China’s Golden Week holiday period.
articles.body:
Global container freight rates remained under pressure in the latest weekly readings, with several major benchmarks declining around China’s Golden Week holiday period.

Drewry’s World Container Index (WCI) fell 2%, while the China Containerized Freight Index (CCFI) and Ningbo Containerized Freight Index (NCFI) also moved lower. The Shanghai Containerized Freight Index (SCFI) was broadly stable, and the Freightos Baltic Index (FBX) recorded almost no change.

At trade-lane level, the latest readings showed mixed conditions across the Transpacific, while Asia-Europe continued its downward trend.

The SCFI edged up 0.05% to 3,664.11 points, compared with 3,662.30 in the previous reading.

The broader CCFI declined 0.6% to 1,912.38 points from 1,923.93.

The NCFI also moved lower, falling approximately 1.5% to 2,431.78 points from 2,468.61 in the previous reading.

The latest figures show that the Chinese benchmarks remain mixed, although two of the three recorded declines.

The latest NYSHEX Freight Index (NYFI) , published on 9 October, showed different movements across the two major Asia-US routes.

Asia-US West Coast declined 1.98% to 7,407.75, reversing the 1.89% increase recorded in the previous reading.

Asia-US East Coast moved in the opposite direction, rising 1.40% to 9,831.24 after remaining almost unchanged in the previous assessment.

Asia-North Europe continued to weaken, falling another 3.24% to 3,356.23.

The Transatlantic market also showed contrasting movements. Westbound rates edged down 0.52% to 2,709.05, while eastbound rates increased 8.23% to 1,282.09.

Drewry’s WCI fell 2% to US$4,351 per 40-foot container in its assessment published on 8 October.

Shanghai-Los Angeles declined 3% to US$7,624 per 40-foot container, while Shanghai-New York fell 2% to US$10,220.

Asia-Europe rates also remained under pressure. Shanghai-Rotterdam decreased 2% to US$3,337, while Shanghai-Genoa was broadly unchanged at US$3,696.

The latest WCI figures indicate softer conditions across both the Transpacific and Asia-Europe trades, although the magnitude of the declines differed between routes.

The assessment coincided with the period around China’s Golden Week holiday, when cargo demand and vessel capacity management can change.

The FBX Global Container Freight Index stood at US$3,344 in its latest weekly reading, virtually unchanged from US$3,343 previously.

Unlike the WCI, which recorded a 2% decrease, the FBX showed little movement at the global level.

The latest readings indicate that the strong Transpacific gains recorded in the previous assessments have given way to a more uneven market.

NYFI’s Asia-US West Coast reading fell 1.98%, while Asia-US East Coast increased 1.40%. Drewry, meanwhile, recorded declines on both Shanghai-Los Angeles and Shanghai-New York.

The indexes use different methodologies and reporting periods, which should be considered when interpreting their respective movements.

Asia-Europe remains the more consistent source of downward pressure.

NYFI’s Asia-North Europe reading declined 3.24%, following a 3.58% decrease in the previous assessment. Drewry also recorded another decline on Shanghai-Rotterdam, although Shanghai-Genoa was broadly stable.

At the composite level, the picture is less uniform. WCI, CCFI and NCFI declined, while SCFI and FBX remained broadly stable.

The different indexes should not be compared directly in absolute terms because they use different methodologies and reporting schedules. However, their latest movements indicate continued pressure across several major freight benchmarks, with particularly persistent weakness on Asia-Europe.

The next readings will provide a clearer indication of freight market conditions following China’s Golden Week.

On the Transpacific, attention will focus on whether the decline recorded on Asia-US West Coast extends to the East Coast and whether the latest WCI decreases continue.

Asia-Europe will remain another important area to monitor. The continued decline in NYFI’s Asia-North Europe reading shows that the route has yet to establish a clear recovery.

Carrier capacity adjustments, including blank sailings, will also be important in determining how available supply develops relative to demand.

For now, the latest readings point to softer conditions across several global freight benchmarks, with uneven Transpacific performance and continued pressure on Asia-Europe.
takeaways: Global container freight rates remained under pressure in the latest weekly readings, with several major benchmarks declining around China’s Golden Week holiday period.
Drewry’s World Container Index (WCI) fell 2%, while the China Containerized Freight Index (CCFI) and Ningbo Containerized Freight Index (NCFI) also moved lower.
The Shanghai Containerized Freight Index (SCFI) was broadly stable, and the Freightos Baltic Index (FBX) recorded almost no change.

articles.title: New wind for hydrogen-electric shipping as GMI-PowerCell collaboration expands to four bulk carriers
articles.summary: PowerCell’s new order to supply hydrogen fuel cell systems for two more GMI bulk carriers brings the total fleet order to four vessels.
articles.body:
PowerCell’s new order to supply hydrogen fuel cell systems for two more GMI bulk carriers brings the total fleet order to four vessels.

Sweden-based high-power-density hydrogen fuel cell stacks and systems developer and manufacturer PowerCell Group has secured a follow-up order from GMI Group, a Norwegian green shipping developer focused on designing and operating zero-emission bulk carriers powered by compressed renewable hydrogen and fuel cell technology, to supply fuel cell systems for two additional hydrogen-electric bulk carriers, doubling the project’s scope from two to four vessels as zero-emission maritime technology transitions from single-ship pilots to standardized fleet deployments.

PowerCell Group has secured a follow-up order worth SEK 27 million ($2.69 million) for fuel cell systems and engineering services for two additional hydrogen-electric bulk carriers for delivery to GMI Group.

The order, which comprises 10 Marine System 225 units, providing more than 2 MW of power, with deliveries scheduled for 2027–2028, follows the first order in September 2025 and expands the collaboration from two to four vessels.

As a result, PowerCell will supply a total of 24 Marine System 225 across the four ships, representing 5.4 MW of installed fuel cell power. GMI Group is developing a new generation of bulk carriers using compressed renewable hydrogen to generate electricity onboard through fuel cells.

Richard Berkling , CEO of PowerCell Group, commented: “Scaling from two vessels to four demonstrates the value of our business model. We combine an industrialised fuel cell platform with application engineering and control capability that can be applied repeatedly across a fleet. This improves delivery efficiency for the customer and expands our installed base for long-term service.”

The first two vessels are 85 meters long, with a deadweight capacity of 4,000 tons, and are planned for launch in 2027. These ships are expected to become the world’s first hydrogen-electric bulk carriers.

The two additional vessels will each have a deadweight capacity of 3,000 tons and will be built by Chowgule Shipyard, with each vessel to be equipped with five Marine System 225.

According to PowerCell, which will provide the fuel cell systems and engineering support within its scope, reusing the same fuel cell platform allows engineering, certification, and integration experience from the first vessels to be applied directly to the subsequent deliveries.

eCap Marine , a German ship integrator specializing in green propulsion solutions, will manage vessel-level integration and certification of the hydrogen and propulsion solution. The vessel concept, which forms part of the Green Shipping Program, has received support from the Norwegian Enova fund and the NOx Fund.

PowerCell underlines that the follow-up order strengthens Marine System 225 as a common platform for larger marine installations and adds another step in the firm’s progression from individual vessel projects to recurring fleet deliveries.

Torstein Holsvik , CEO of GMI Group, said: “The decision to add two vessels reflects our confidence in the solution and in the cooperation established through the first project.

“Using the same core technology and delivery structure gives us a strong basis for developing a new generation of bulk carriers powered by renewable hydrogen.”

Maersk will increase its Import and Export Fuel Surcharge for US inland haulage from 1 November 2026.

The Maersk US inland fuel surcharge will rise from US$140 to US$215 per container.

The revised surcharge will apply to shipments carried under a Maersk ocean bill of lading when the carrier arranges trucking to or from the customer’s door within the United States.

It will apply to shipments with a Price Calculation Date on or after 1 November 2026. The charge will appear separately on the bill of lading under the IFS or EFS code.

Maersk attributed the adjustment to rising US diesel prices. The carrier said the 13-week average diesel price increased by more than US$0.10 per gallon, adding pressure to linehaul, drayage, depot and first-mile transportation costs.

articles.summary: Singapore-listed Yangzijiang Maritime Development has struck a bulk carrier newbuilding deal in China, for up to six kamsarmaxes at Jiangsu Watts Energy & Engineering.
articles.body:
Singapore-listed Yangzijiang Maritime Development has struck a bulk carrier newbuilding deal in China, for up to six kamsarmaxes at Jiangsu Watts Energy & Engineering.

The Ren Yuanlin-led maritime investment group has signed for four firm 82,000 dwt vessels, with options for another two, according to Chinese shipbuilding sources.

The deal would mark Yangzijiang Maritime’s first reported order at Watts, which has only recently entered conventional merchant ship construction.

In August, the Qidong-based yard secured its first kamsarmax contract from Xiamen-based Amoysailing Maritime, covering four 82,000 dwt vessels for delivery in 2028.

That contract was estimated at around $35m to $38m per vessel for standard specifications, although no pricing has surfaced for the latest reported Yangzijiang Maritime series.

The order adds another chapter to Yangzijiang Maritime’s aggressive expansion across several shipping segments.

In September, the company formally disclosed 24 firm newbuilding contracts and 16 options spread across five vessel types, including six 64,500 dwt ultramaxes, six MR product and chemical tankers, eight stainless steel chemical tankers and four VLCCs.

That programme lifted its disclosed newbuilding portfolio to 98 vessels, comprising 75 firm ships under construction, 16 options and seven vessels already delivered.

The latest kamsarmax deal would represent a separate move into larger dry bulk tonnage rather than an additional disclosure of the previously announced ultramax programme.

Yangzijiang Maritime has increasingly turned to smaller Chinese yards to secure competitively priced newbuildings, combining its shipbuilding investments with chartering, leasing and pre-delivery vessel sales.

The company has also been expanding its tanker exposure, with its reported programme at Jiangsu Haifeng Shipbuilding now covering six firm and two optional 114,000 dwt LR2s.

Scotland-headquartered offshore drilling contractor Stena Drilling has confirmed the departure of its 2008-built drillship from a Spanish shipyard in the Canary Islands to embark on its voyage to Namibia, where it will begin its next assignment.

Stena Drilling has announced that Stena DrillMAX , which departed Las Palmas, is now en route to Namibia for the drillship’s next campaign.

The rig owner highlighted: “With preparations complete, we look forward to seeing her begin operations in Namibia. Safe travels to everyone onboard!”

No information about the exact well the drillship will work on is currently available, but it is expected to be deployed on PEL 39 , which is operated by Shell in partnership with QatarEnergy and NAMCOR.

Following the Merlin discovery, the operator continues to evaluate its results, which indicate a good-quality reservoir with light oil and limited associated gas. Shell said in April 2026 that further drilling was under consideration as part of a broader exploratory appraisal program.

Once the drilling work in Namibia is done, the Stena DrillMAX drillship is expected to move to its assignment with Energean in the Mediterranean. The 2008-built harsh environment DP Class 3 drillship is capable of drilling in water depths up to 10,000 feet.

With a maximum drilling depth of 35,000 ft, the drillship can accommodate 180 people. This rig became the first drillship to be awarded DNV’s Abate (P) notation back in December 2023.

Stena Drilling’s rig fleet is deployed for work across geographies, as illustrated by its 2012-built Stena IceMAX drillship, which recently completed a three-well campaign in Egypt’s Western Mediterranean region.

The UK affiliate of Sweden’s Saab emphasizes that Ørsted relies on advanced subsea technology to help monitor the integrity of critical infrastructure, including foundations, cables, and other submerged assets.

According to the ROV player, remotely operated vehicles play a vital role in these operations, enabling efficient inspections and maintenance activities that help maximize asset availability and support energy generation.

Saab UK’s Seaeye ROVs have operated in some of the world's most demanding subsea environments for more than four decades, with Cougar XT Compact continuing that heritage to assist those responsible for maintaining the infrastructure that supports the global energy transition.

Estonian outfit Klip Marine is reportedly exiting the segment by selling the Ekaterini V (173,555 dwt, built 2012 at Bohai Shipbuilding) to Chinese buyers for $35m, with its special survey and drydocking due in January.

Another deal quietly slipped under the headlines that month: Sunrising International, an outfit known for trading older secondhand tonnage, exited the capesize segment by selling the 20-year-old Highland (174,092 dwt) for $25m; the ship was added for around $15m in early 2024.

The increased buying interest comes against a firmer market backdrop, with Clarksons recently noting that its iron ore indicator was up around 6% year-on-year.

articles.title: Ship recycling drought leaves record ageing fleet afloat
articles.summary: Ship recycling has sunk into its longest sustained slump in more than half a century, just as the global merchant fleet accumulates an unprecedented amount of ageing tonnage.
articles.body:
Ship recycling has sunk into its longest sustained slump in more than half a century, just as the global merchant fleet accumulates an unprecedented amount of ageing tonnage.

Clarksons Research calculates that just 273 ships of 5.5m gt, equivalent to around 8m dwt, were sold for demolition in the first nine months of 2026, 13% below last year’s already dismal pace and 60% beneath the average across the 2000s and 2010s.

Less than 0.5% of global fleet tonnage has been scrapped annually for five successive years, a lower rate even than during the 2006-08 supercycle and the longest such drought since the early 1970s.

As a consequence, more than 340m gt of shipping is now at least 20 years old, up 90% in five years and representing almost 20% of the world fleet, compared with 12% in 2021. Over 150m gt is aged 25 or more, up 75% in five years, while a record 68m gt has passed 30 years.

More than 340m gt of shipping is now at least 20 years old, up 90% in five years

The situation is particularly pronounced in tankers: 22% of capacity is now over 20 years old, against just 8% five years ago. In containers, the proportion has doubled to 16%, even as an orderbook exceeding 40% of the existing fleet looms. By comparison, only 12% of bulk carrier capacity and 10% of LNG tonnage is over 20 years old.

The economics of demolition remain unpersuasive in the record-setting freight rate era of the 2020s. Indian subcontinent scrap steel prices have risen 20-25% this year, but the ClarkSea Index hit another all-time high of $84,951 a day on Friday, making continued employment and secondhand sales vastly more attractive.

Clarksons’ latest recycling market assessment records just 8.4m dwt sold for demolition year-to-date. It notes continuing buying interest in Bangladesh and Pakistan, while Indian recyclers favour specialised tonnage.

Cash buyer GMS stated in its latest weekly report: “The final quarter is … developing into a contest of patience. Recyclers have the capacity and willingness to buy, but owners still have freight earnings, secondhand alternatives and time on their side.”

The growing stockpile of elderly vessels could ultimately provide shipping with a substantial supply-side release valve when freight markets eventually correct.
takeaways: Ship recycling has sunk into its longest sustained slump in more than half a century, just as the global merchant fleet accumulates an unprecedented amount of ageing tonnage.
Less than 0.5% of global fleet tonnage has been scrapped annually for five successive years, a lower rate even than during the 2006-08 supercycle and the longest such drought since the early 1970s.
As a consequence, more than 340m gt of shipping is now at least 20 years old, up 90% in five years and representing almost 20% of the world fleet, compared with 12% in 2021.

articles.title: Shipping’s extraordinary boom refuses to peak
articles.summary: Global shipping earnings have reached another extraordinary milestone, with Clarksons Research’s cross-sector ClarkSea Index surging 12% in a week to an unprecedented $84,951 a day, its fifth consecutive all-time high.
articles.body:
Global shipping earnings have reached another extraordinary milestone, with Clarksons Research’s cross-sector ClarkSea Index surging 12% in a week to an unprecedented $84,951 a day, its fifth consecutive all-time high.

The index, a widely followed overall earnings barometer, measures average daily earnings across tankers, bulk carriers, containerships and gas carriers, weighted by vessel numbers in each sector. It covers approximately 80% of global shipping capacity, providing a broad measure of the industry’s fortunes.

The latest reading dwarfs the previous shipping supercycle’s 2007 peak of $50,714 a day. This year’s average is running 70% above 2025 and 87% ahead of the ten-year trend.

Crude tankers are driving the latest surge.

Average VLCC earnings jumped another 21% last week to $804,601 a day, while suezmaxes climbed 17% to $724,398 and aframaxes surged 46% to $393,951.

Elsewhere, dry bulk has softened, with capesize earnings retreating 16% to $31,130 and overall bulker earnings slipping 3% to $22,319.

Containers remain exceptionally resilient. The Shanghai Containerised Freight Index stands at 3,664 points, 215% higher year-on-year.

VLGCs are enjoying record earnings, reaching $209,000 a day on the US Gulf-Japan route, although LNG carriers remain the conspicuous laggard, with modern spot earnings down 19% to $34,250.

Discussing today’s sky-high earnings, broker Hartland noted in a new report: “Wars in Europe and the Middle East have rendered the Middle East Gulf, Red Sea and Black Sea unsafe for shipping, not that shipping is much deterred. The present boom is universal, transcending shipping sectors, as demand remains robust and ton-miles have been added as ships detour around war zones by taking longer routes home. All shipping sectors have been unwitting beneficiaries of war.?

Researchers at another broker Affinity stated in a recent report: “With this cycle now being well into at least its 5th or 6th year, it might seem the wrong time for newbuilding demand to be so robust. But this cycle is being driven by the geopolitical environment which show no signs of abating…There’s still more life in this party yet.”

articles.title: Tanker war spreads across Gulf
articles.summary: Attacks on commercial shipping are spreading across the Gulf region, with two Indian seafarers missing after a drone struck a tanker off Oman on Sunday and another tanker hit by a projectile while exiting the Strait of...
articles.body:
Attacks on commercial shipping are spreading across the Gulf region, with two Indian seafarers missing after a drone struck a tanker off Oman on Sunday and another tanker hit by a projectile while exiting the Strait of Hormuz.

The Nicaragua-flagged Petro Dolphin was attacked at Sohar Anchorage on Sunday. India’s minister for ports, shipping and waterways, Sarbananda Sonowal, confirmed that nine of the 11 Indian crew had been rescued, while two remained missing. Omani authorities have launched a search and rescue operation.

UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) confirmed the drone attack, initially reporting the incident as suspicious activity before reclassifying it following confirmation that the vessel had been struck by an unmanned aerial vehicle.

A growing number of sanctioned vessels operating around the Strait of Hormuz are broadcasting Nicaraguan identities, raising fresh questions about the spread of questionable ship registrations as maritime warfare intensifies across the Middle East.

New research from maritime tracking platform HullCipher has identified 10 blacklisted ships that began broadcasting Nicaraguan Maritime Mobile Service Identity (MMSI) numbers between August 1 and September 26.

Earlier this year, investigative organisation Bellingcat identified a website offering ship registrations purportedly on behalf of Nicaragua, despite International Maritime Organization records showing no organisation authorised to issue registrations for the country.

Separately, the Marshall Islands-flagged tanker Valthera came under attack in the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday, with an unidentified projectile causing a fire onboard. Sonowal confirmed all 11 Indian crew members were safe.

UKMTO reported an outbound tanker struck on its port side on Sunday, with no pollution reported. The agency had recorded another tanker strike in the strait on Saturday evening, also involving a projectile and onboard fire.

The latest violence follows Friday’s attack on the Panama-flagged, 302,000 dwt Gem No.2, struck around 13 nautical miles west of Al Jazeera, UAE.

Maritime security firm Vanguard identified the vessel, which is managed in Taiwan and linked to U-Ming Marine Transport. Sonowal confirmed that all 22 Indian seafarers onboard were safe. A fire was extinguished, although the extent of damage remains unclear.

Another tanker was struck off Qatar last week as Iran’s Revolutionary Guards warned they would pursue ships taking unauthorised routes anywhere in the region, rather than just inside Hormuz.

The guards have also claimed attacks on the Vietnamese LPG carrier NV Sunshine and a VLCC allegedly damaged by a naval mine. Neither claim has been independently verified.

Meanwhile, US forces struck the Panama-flagged bulker Ocean Molica, also known as Arika Sun, in the Gulf of Oman on Saturday, disabling its propulsion after it allegedly ignored warnings under Washington’s blockade of Iranian ports. No injuries were reported.

articles.body:
Galdor Exploration has forged a pact with TGS, combining subsurface expertise with cutting-edge AI to rewrite the playbook for North Sea discoveries.

In a move that enables artificial intelligence (AI) to get a stronger foothold in the North Sea, Norway’s energy data and intelligence company TGS has inked a strategic framework agreement with newly minted Galdor Exploration to deploy proprietary seismic foundation models and next-generation machine learning workflows to unearth overlooked subsurface potential across the Norwegian Continental Shelf (NCS).

TGS has entered into a framework agreement for a strategic collaboration with Galdor Exploration, a company formally established on July 19, 2026, coinciding symbolically with the 60th anniversary of the spudding of Norway’s first exploration well, to unlock high-value exploration opportunities on the Norwegian Continental Shelf and the broader North Sea region through the application of advanced, integrated data solutions and artificial intelligence.

Kristian Johansen , CEO of TGS, commented: “This collaboration reflects our commitment to supporting the next generation of exploration companies with the highest-quality data and cutting-edge exploration technology. By working in a different, more collaborative way with our customers, applying the full scope of our integrated solutions, we aim to accelerate value creation and deliver win-win results.” As Galdor Exploration is set on a modern, data-driven exploration strategy that combines advanced AI-enabled workflows with the multidisciplinary expertise of a highly experienced exploration team with an extensive track record on the NCS and internationally, this collaboration will give the firm access to TGS’ integrated data and technology solutions across the energy data value chain. The duo will also work together to implement advanced AI exploration workflows and solutions. Ørjan Gjerde , CEO and Founder of Galdor Exploration, underlined: “Galdor’s strategy is built on a conviction that the future of exploration lies in a modern exploration organization, where we combine deep exploration experience with premium subsurface data and next-generation AI-enabled workflows.

“Our collaboration with TGS gives us access to data, technology and expertise of exceptional breadth and quality and allows us to apply advanced machine learning exploration techniques at scale. This will support Galdor’s goal to identify and mature exploration opportunities that, by using conventional approaches, may have been overlooked, underestimated or left behind.”

TGS recently won multiple deals and begun jobs, such as a high-resolution data upgrade assignment to support future well planning and reservoir evaluation at an offshore discovery in Malaysian waters.

articles.title: Shell and Equinor fuel $1.1 billion backlog uptick for Transocean
articles.summary: Transocean gets its hands on a North Sea contract for a semi-submersible with Shell and a final approval for three rigs from Equinor.
articles.body:
Transocean gets its hands on a North Sea contract for a semi-submersible with Shell and a final approval for three rigs from Equinor.

Switzerland-based offshore drilling contractor Transocean has tucked under its belt a combined $1.1 billion in offshore commitments, bolstered by a fresh North Sea deal with A/S Norske Shell, a subsidiary of the UK-headquartered energy giant Shell, and the official final approval of a massive three-rig agreement with the Norwegian state-owned energy heavyweight Equinor off the coast of Norway.

The Transocean Norge semi-submersible rig has won a two-well contract with A/S Norske Shell. The estimated 120 days of work is expected to begin in direct continuation of the rig's previously awarded programs in Norway and contribute approximately $62 million in backlog, excluding additional services.

This contract also includes one single-well option. Transocean Norge is said to be the first semi-submersible rig that secured the Abate (Power+) notation for greenhouse gas abatement.

With a maximum drilling depth of 40,000 feet, the 2019-built sixth-generation Moss Maritime CS60 semi-submersible rig was constructed at Jurong Shipyard in Singapore and can accommodate 150 people.

In late September, the rig owner received final approval from Equinor for the previously announced agreement for three harsh environment semi-submersible rigs in Norway, including the 2016-built Transocean Enabler , the 2015-built Transocean Encourage , and the 2015-built Transocean Endurance units.

As a result, Transocean has locked in a contract backlog of approximately $1.1 billion with a new contract award representing around $62 million in firm contract backlog and the formal approval of the previously announced agreement with Equinor, resulting in the conversion of the $1 billion contract value to firm backlog.

This backlog addition comes less than two months after Transocean got a long-term deal for a 2010-built ultra-deepwater drillship with India’s government-owned energy giant Oil and Natural Gas Corporation (ONGC).
